speechtext:
That was the last figure I had, and it may be lower than that. During the last election campaign in the United States the figure of 10,000,000 was given. But if there are only 6,000,000 unemployed, that means there are plenty of men there for us to employ.
The minister talks of increasing our exports as a means of overcoming our exchange difficulties. In that he is on safe ground. He fears to subsidize exports lest he encounter difficulties with the United States.
There are indirect ways of helping to increase our exports. One of these is to decrease the cost of production, thereby lowering the price of our goods for export. Why not so manage that there would be lower interest rates on loans; why not consider the remission of freight rates and the application of discounts to the prices of goods used in production?
For example, in the use of mill feeds. (Some hon. members smile about this pro-

posal. Last spring, Mr. Speaker, we gave to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and to the government absolute powers. If they have not used these powers to make the necessary adjustments, then so much more the reflection upon them because this parliament has done its share.) Why not a sales tax remission on goods entering into production so as to bring down costs and enable us to sell our goods on foreign markets? If we use our national credit, our goods-and-services producing and consuming powers, to increase production and modify the price structure, we shall be able to convert this country into a veritable arsenal to support the empire in war, and a veritable storehouse of goods to sustain our war effort.
May I commend the minister for his desire to assist Britain? We must help Britain; we must give Britain far more assistance than we can possibly expect Britain to pay for by sending over to us some of her bituminous coal and what-not. How are we going to do it? I say that Canada can assist Great Britain without debt to us, without taxation, and without taking away anything from our people, and she can give Britain goods up to the limit of Canada's ability to produce, so that the contrast between what we could do and what we are doing now would be enormous. We do not need to take Britain's bituminous coal or her other goods, fine gesture as it was on the minister's part to offer to do that. Does Britain need for other purposes her workers who are producing her coal? If she does, then in taking her coal we are causing her to put to work labourers who might be better employed. If she is not using those labourers, why not bring them to Canada and put them to work here?
We have in Canada, Mr. Speaker, a tremendous capacity for producing iron. Some people may say that our ore deposits are remote. Then why not bring them up close? Yes, laugh, with your prehistoric minds and antiquated thinking, but if the proposal were advanced that Hitler should have control of the Labrador iron fields, we should immediately become fearful because we know that Hitler would use them. How is it that Hitler could use them, and we cannot, when they are so much closer to us than they would be to him?
We have a tremendous capacity for producing iron and a wide variety of other products such as eggs, wood and lumber, copper, nickel, fruits, cheese; and all these things could be bought with Canada's credit and given to Britain in so far as we produce more of them than we ourselves need, and in so far as we can produce other goods which

War Budget

Mr. Blackmore
would absorb the money which would have to be created by Canada and spent to buy the iron, etcetera, in Canada.
May I say a word or two with respect to the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well). We are going to support that amendment. Our social crediters believe in debt-free money. This proposal has been refused by the minister, but perhaps he will live to wonder why in the world he could ever have thought that it was not a sound proposal.
Social crediters took the stand last year that we should have conscription of finance, industry and man-power. By conscription of finance we meant that the government should take over the power and the function of turning into money Canada's goods-and-services producing and consuming power, that the government should monetize Canada's credit. Once that were done, the amount of money at the government's disposal would be highly gratifying I am sure to the Minister of Finance. We felt that if that were done, it would be unnecessary to conscript industry because a government can control industry through the technique of prices, and it would be unnecessary to conscript man-power because men will go to-day where they can get money enough. So that was our proposal.
The government must have money, and money that is interest-free because the interest burden on this country is rapidly becoming so colossal that it is causing anxiety to all serious thinkers. Since our own proposal was refused, we intend to back the proposal that has been made this afternoon by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, that those who are able to lend money, who have it to spare, who are not using it for production or for economic consumption in Canada, should be called upon to lend the money interest-free to the nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON PROPOSALS OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR CONSERVATION OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Is that what it means?

speechtext:
I take it that that
is what it means. I have not asked them what it means, but the words mean that to me. It merely proposes to borrow the money. That is not so bad as conscripting our young men. If I had $100,000 that I was not doing anything with, I would rather a hundred times that the government ask me to lend it to the nation without interest than that they ask me that I give one of my precious sons. It is a simple proposal. It might be pointed out that in the army a man is earning $1.30 a day, but I think I could arrange matters so that he could earn more than that outside the army, and so could any other man in Canada who is well situated.
I do not think the proposal contained in the amendment would be a serious handicap
to the Canadian people, although I wish to point out that the social credit concept does not envisage the taking away of money from the people.
I have given the reasons why I am going to support the amendment. I have also put my case with respect to the minister's budget. I wish to commend him for the moderation of the budget. I wish to commend him for all the various things I have mentioned, and I will say that considering the circumstances in which he is situated, the budget does him a great deal of credit. On the other hand I have pointed out the reasons why I oppose it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON PROPOSALS OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR CONSERVATION OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question just to clarify his position? He says he would not take money away from the people, but he would be in favour of a compulsory loan to the government. How does he reconcile those two statements?

convey to the minister what I was trying to say, that is, that social credit as a philosophy does not envisage taking money away from people. But we are going to support the amendment moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, not because it is in accordance with social credit principles but because it offers a means whereby the government can obtain money without interest. Have I made that quite clear?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON PROPOSALS OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR CONSERVATION OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE

position is that the hon. member does not support the amendment as a matter of social credit philosophy or principle, but is supporting the proposal in this instance.

lesser of two evils. The minister is proposing one very serious evil, and the proposal in the amendment is a little bit less evil than some of the minister's proposals.
